question: Should public conservation money go towards bringing extinct species back to life?
answer: Revival draws money that would never reach conservation otherwise: private investors have put hundreds of millions into de-extinction companies. The tools it builds, from frozen cell banks to gene edits for disease resistance, already help endangered living species. A revived grazer or seed-spreader can also restore ecological roles that have been empty for centuries.
move: Whichever side you took, it turns on whether revival money would exist otherwise.
ask: When someone offers money for a flashy cause, do I ask whether it would exist for the unflashy one?
counterpoint: Bennett and colleagues costed revival for New Zealand and New South Wales: keeping revived species alive in the wild would absorb money that could protect more living species, a net loss of biodiversity. A revived animal also needs the habitat and safety whose absence killed it the first time. Rescue is cheaper before the last one dies.
source: Bennett et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2017
reference: Bennett et al., Spending limited resources on de-extinction could lead to net biodiversity loss, Nature Ecology & Evolution, 2017
